en.title: Atonement: How Boyd Holbrook Seeks Peace After War's Unspeakable Cost
en.summary: Reed Van Dyk's powerful war drama, 'Atonement,' forces audiences to confront the devastating ripple effects of violence. Starring Boyd Holbrook and Hiam Abbass, the film explores the agonizing journey toward forgiveness in the wake of tragedy.
en.body:
## The Weight of a Trigger Pull

In **Reed Van Dyk's** unflinching drama **“Atonement,”** the shattering impact of a single, ill-fated decision unfolds with gut-wrenching clarity. Based on **Dexter Filkins'** poignant 2012 New Yorker article, the film eschews the typical bombast of war movies, opting instead for a deeply personal exploration of trauma and its lingering shadows. We first meet a family in Iraq, their lives a tapestry of ordinary moments woven with warmth and quiet dignity, captured beautifully on 16mm film by cinematographer **Jon Peter**. This extended period of peace makes the sudden, violent explosion that obliterates their world all the more visceral. It’s a testament to Van Dyk’s direction that when the film inevitably turns to the horrors of war, the audience feels not adrenaline, but a profound sense of lament for the lives irrevocably shattered.

The nightmare becomes a brutal reality for matriarch **Mariam Khachaturian** (played with immense depth by **Hiam Abbass**), who flees with her family only to witness her husband and children gunned down by a trigger-happy U.S. Marine, **Lou D’Alessandro** (a compelling **Boyd Holbrook**). Mistaken for insurgents, their deaths are a catastrophic error, a moment that will haunt Lou and his unit for years to come. Years later, grappling with the immense fallout of that day, Lou learns of a journalist, **Michael Reid** (portrayed by **Kenneth Branagh**), who has written about the killings, identifying Mariam and her daughter Nora (Gheed) as the sole survivors. This discovery sets Lou on a desperate path to seek absolution, to atone for his sins.

## The Long Road to Forgiveness

**“Atonement”** distinguishes itself by refusing to let Mariam and her family exist merely as plot devices in Lou’s redemption arc. The film centers their experience, allowing us to feel the immeasurable weight of their loss and the deep scars, both mental and physical, that Mariam carries. Her journey is one of profound internal struggle: can she, or even *will* she, offer peace to the man who destroyed her world, even as she navigates her own fractured existence? This delicate dance between perpetrator and victim, between the desire for justice and the possibility of grace, forms the emotional core of the film. It asks difficult questions about accountability, the nature of forgiveness, and whether true atonement is ever truly attainable.

## What's Next

Having premiered at the Directors’ Fortnight at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival and released on October 2, 2026, **“Atonement”** is now available for audiences to experience. The film’s powerful performances and its thoughtful, humanistic approach to a difficult subject matter are sure to spark conversation among viewers and critics alike.

content_raw: From the opening moments of director Reed Van Dyk’s “ Atonement ,” the film subverts tropes and expands what war films (and their harrowing aftermath) can be. Shot on a warm, 16mm film by cinematographer Jon Peter, the film opens with a family in Iraq going about their quotidian rhythms for an extended period of time before an explosion shatters their peace. We feel the surprise just as viscerally as the family does. Even if war films try to be anti-war, you feel the fundamental tension when those projects dedicate screen time and craft to make the battle scenes robust while leaving the human drama behind. Not so for “Atonement,” by the time the film transitions to its scenes depicting war, you feel lament, because you’ve grown to love the family whose lives are now being torn apart. Nightmare becomes reality for matriarch Mariam Khachaturian, who flees with her family after the explosion, only to see her children and husband get gunned down by U.S. Marine Lou D’Alessandro (Boyd Holbrook), who, being far too trigger-happy, mistook them for “enemy” Iraqis. Years after, Lou and his crew wrestle with the traumatic fallout of their murders, and in their grief, Lou learns that journalist Michael Reid (Kenneth Branagh) has written an article about the killings, citing Mariam and her daughter, Nora (Gheed), as the only survivors. Lou seeks to contact them to atone for his sins, while Miriam wrestles with whether she is ready to offer peace even while nursing the mental and physical scars of their encounter. Van Dyk adapted the film from Dexter Filkin’s New Yorker article of the same name, and while other films might focus solely on Lou, treating Mariam, Nora, and their families as voiceless secondary characters, whose roles in the narrative are to act as cogs in Lou’s redemption arc, Van Dyk ensures all characters have fully fleshed-out arcs, offering no easy answers right down to its beautifully tender final shot. While the film made its Canadian premiere during this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, RogerEbert.com sat down with Van Dyk, Holbrook, Abbass, and Branagh; these interviews have been edited in three parts and combined into one fluid conversation. The foursome discuss changing the grammar of war films, the ways modern conceptions of mercy have been shaped by Shakespeare, and the key Biblical verse that served as a springboard of sorts for the film’s thorny exploration of forgiveness. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity. Reed, I know that you wanted to shoot this film in Baghdad and though that was not a possibility, you did visit with your cinematographer, Jon Peter. Can you speak more to that trip, how it shaped your approach to filming in Amman, Jordan? Reed Van Dyk: Through the making of the film, I got very close with several Iraqi filmmakers, and also Gheed.
